sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Good morning everyone, let's get started.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Last week we finished our review of functions, and today we begin the first really new idea of this course, which is the limit.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Here is the plan for today.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: First I want to give you the idea of a limit in plain words.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Then we will look at a famous example, sine x over x.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: After that we will talk about one-sided limits, and finally about when a limit does not exist.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: By the end of the hour you should be able to read a limit statement and say in your own words what it means.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: So what is a limit?

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: A limit describes the value a function approaches as the input approaches some point.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Notice that I said approaches, not equals.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: The function does not even need to be defined at that point.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Think about walking toward a door.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: With every step you cover half of the remaining distance.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: You get closer and closer to the door, but you never actually step through it.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: The door is the limit of your position.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: We write it like this: the limit of f of x, as x approaches a, equals L.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Read it out loud with me: the limit of f of x, as x approaches a, equals L.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: The letter a is where the input is heading, and the letter L is where the output is heading.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Does that make sense to everyone?

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Okay, good, let's keep going.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Now for the famous example.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Take the function f of x equals sine x divided by x.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: What happens if we plug in zero?

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: We get zero over zero, which is not defined, so the function has no value at zero.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: But we can still ask what the function is approaching.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Look at the table on this slide.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: When x is zero point five, the ratio is about zero point nine five nine.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: When x is zero point one, it is about zero point nine nine eight.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: When x is zero point zero one, it is zero point nine nine nine nine eight.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: The ratio gets closer and closer to one.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: So what does this limit equal?

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Right, it equals one.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: On the graph you can see a smooth curve with a tiny hole at the point zero comma one.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: The hole is exactly the door from our picture: the curve walks up to it from both sides and never steps through.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: We will prove this properly next week, so for today just trust the table.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Before we move on, I want you to try one yourselves.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Take thirty seconds and work out, with your neighbour, what x squared minus one over x minus one approaches as x goes to one.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Okay, what did you get?

sentences.speaker: student
sentences.text: We factored the top, so it cancels and you get x plus one, and that goes to two.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Exactly, the factor x minus one cancels, and what is left is x plus one, which approaches two.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: And did anyone try a table instead?

sentences.speaker: student
sentences.text: We did, we tried zero point nine and one point one and got one point nine and two point one.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Good, so two different methods agree, and that should make you more confident in the answer.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Notice again that the function is not defined at one, and the limit does not care.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Now let us move on to one-sided limits.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Sometimes it matters which direction you come from.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: The left-hand limit means x approaches a from below, through smaller values.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: The right-hand limit means x approaches a from above, through larger values.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: The two-sided limit exists only if both sides agree.

sentences.speaker: student
sentences.text: Is the left limit always the same as the right limit?

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Good question, and the answer is no.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Think of the step function, which is zero for negative inputs and one for positive inputs.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: From the left you are walking along the floor at height zero.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: From the right you are walking along a shelf at height one.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: So the left-hand limit is zero and the right-hand limit is one.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: They disagree, so we say the two-sided limit at zero does not exist.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Why do we care about this?

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Because later, when we define continuity and the derivative, both of them are built out of limits that must agree from both sides.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Any questions about one-sided limits?

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: No? Okay.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Let me summarise what we did today.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: A limit is about approaching, not arriving.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: The function does not need to be defined at the point.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: And before you claim that a limit exists, check both sides.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: For practice, please do problems one to six on the worksheet before Thursday.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Problems five and six are one-sided limits, so look back at the step function if you get stuck.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Next time we will learn the limit laws, which let us compute limits without building a table every time.

sentences.speaker: teacher
sentences.text: Thank you, see you on Thursday.

The idea of a limit

The function does not need to be defined at that point

One-sided limits

Right-hand limit: x approaches a from above
The two-sided limit exists only if both sides agree
